paragraphs.source_en: No sooner had Mr. Ato from the Suzuki household left than Dr. Amaki came in. Since ancient times, people who are short-tempered and call themselves short-tempered have been rare. By the time one notices that something is a little wrong with oneself, one has generally already passed the peak of one's fit of anger. My master's fit of anger reached its highest pitch during yesterday's great incident, and though the negotiations ended in an anticlimax, they were somehow settled after all. That evening, as he sat in his study and thought it over, he realized that the matter was rather abnormal. Whether it was Rakuenkan that was abnormal, or he himself, was of course still quite open to doubt. At any rate, abnormal it certainly was. At the same time, he also realized that although he lived next door to a middle school, it was indeed somewhat abnormal to keep losing his temper all year round like this. Since it was abnormal, something had to be done about it. Yet though he said something had to be done, in the end there was nothing to do. There was no course except to take some medicine from a doctor and treat his disease of being irritable. Having understood this, he conceived the idea of asking Dr. Amaki, with whom he was long acquainted, to examine him. Whether my master was wise or foolish may be left aside; in any case, the mere fact that he noticed his own fit of anger deserves admiration, and must be called a singularly commendable thought. Dr. Amaki, as usual, smiled with perfect composure and said, “How are you? What seems to be the trouble?” Doctors, as a rule, always say, “What seems to be the trouble?” As for a doctor who does not say, “What seems to be the trouble?” I cannot bring myself to trust him.
